competency.title: Lead in public: listen, decide, own the call, and run a meeting people trust

name: Civic Leadership and Emotional Intelligence

stations.why: The shared opener: standing up in public with a case that is sourced, timed and respectful is the first civic skill every station here builds on.
The briefing before the stations: the eight principles stated honestly, the decision framework they hang on, and the open-meeting, disclosure and access law every station after it assumes.
Chairing the meeting is where listening first becomes a procedure: every speaker heard to the bell, nothing acted on that was not noticed, and each vote stated aloud.
Keeping your word is learned one resident at a time, at a counter where the only honest promise is a date the office can actually meet.
A coalition table is where a leader learns to find the interest behind each position and to count support honestly without carrying votes between officials.
Closing a budget gap in front of the people it lands on is the plainest test of spending public money in the open and owning the hard call.
Disclosure, gifts, recusal and the revolving door are where a leader's word is tested when nobody would have noticed otherwise.
The podium on the worst day asks for every principle at once: confirm before you speak, reach everybody, and correct a mistake in public.
A listening session with nothing to defend is where bringing people in rather than shutting them out is practised as a skill rather than a slogan.
Mediating between two neighbours trains the emotional intelligence underneath every other station: hear each side whole, take the blame out, and keep the room level.
The programme ends where leadership does, with the seat handed on to somebody who can do the job without you.

The clerk's side of the open meeting, where the Brown Act is kept or lost before the chair ever speaks: an agenda the public could actually read, a quorum counted honestly, and a closed session kept to what was noticed and reported out.
A registration table on a Saturday plaza is where bringing people in rather than shutting them out is practised one voter at a time, with the table belonging to every party and to none.

The morning after an earthquake, leadership is a block captain working inside the volunteer's role: rescuer safety first, a report up one chain, and the list of who needs help kept off the group chat.
Keeping a restorative circle is listening first taken as far as it goes, with the talking piece's rule held, speaking time kept fair and the harm named without shaming the person who did it.

Asking for public money and accounting for it is the other side of spending it in the open: a budget that means something, a conflict disclosed and recused, and a report that claims only what it can prove.
The hardest seat in the programme is the one where the harm was yours, and owning it across language, age and experience is where emotional intelligence stops being a slogan.
Two crew members clash beside live traffic, and the lead notices it, names it, slows it down behind the barrier and gets both of them to a fix they will actually work under.

Feedback that names the behaviour rather than the person is only half the skill; the other half is hearing, in the same conversation, that your own instruction was the gap and taking it without defending.
When the schedule slips and the crew is tired, a lead keeps them steady with a calm voice, one clear next step and no safety step traded for time, then hands the credit to the crew by name.

summary: Stations that teach the decisions a leader makes in public: listening before speaking, naming the interest behind a position, running a meeting people trust, spending a budget in the open, taking a hard call and owning it, and the emotional intelligence that makes each of those possible.
union: SEIU and AFSCME public-service staff, the trades' own apprenticeship coordinators, and community organisations that train residents for public life
